# 2.4-2 Graphical Understanding of Convolution

%%KC_BLOCK%%<section class="convolution-stage-intro" data-convolution-stage-intro="true"><p class="convolution-stage-kicker">SECTION 2.4-2</p><h2>Graphical Convolution</h2><p class="convolution-overview-objective">Interpret and compute continuous-time convolution graphically.</p><div class="convolution-overview-formula" data-convolution-overview-formula>\(c(t)=\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)g(t-\tau)\,d\tau\)</div><div class="convolution-core-actions"><div data-convolution-core-action="flip-slide"><strong>Flip and slide</strong><span>Build the moving signal.</span></div><div data-convolution-core-action="multiply"><strong>Multiply</strong><span>Keep only point-by-point overlap.</span></div><div data-convolution-core-action="integrate"><strong>Integrate</strong><span>Turn product area into one output value.</span></div></div><button class="convolution-intro-start" type="button" data-convolution-intro-start>Start Lesson <span aria-hidden="true">→</span></button></section>%%KC_END%%

%%KC_BLOCK%%<div class="kc-visual-meta" data-visual-kind="guided_convolution" data-teaching-role="concept_anchor" style="display:none;"></div>%%KC_END%%

## 1. What Is Convolution?

%%KC_BLOCK%%<section class="convolution-teaching-block convolution-block-input" data-convolution-page="1"><div class="convolution-block-body"><p class="convolution-page-question">How can every earlier input affect the output now?</p><div class="convolution-equation">\(c(t)=\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)g(t-\tau)\,d\tau\)</div><ul><li><span class="convolution-key convolution-key-input">\(x(\tau)\)</span> tells us how much input arrived at past time \(\tau\).</li><li><span class="convolution-key convolution-key-response">\(g(t-\tau)\)</span> tells us how much of that input's effect remains at time \(t\).</li><li>The integral <span class="convolution-key convolution-key-output">adds all surviving effects</span>.</li></ul><div class="convolution-analogy-layout"><div><h3>Ink in a transparent pool</h3><ul><li>Add ink one drop at a time.</li><li>Each drop spreads and fades, but does not vanish at once.</li><li>The color now is the sum of every earlier drop still visible.</li></ul></div><figure class="convolution-analogy-figure"><img class="lesson-img convolution-analogy-image" src="/lesson-illustrations/2_4-2/convolution-ink-memory-v2.png" data-api-asset="1" alt="Ink drops spreading and accumulating in a transparent pool" width="1153" height="2048" loading="lazy" decoding="async"></figure></div></div></section>%%KC_END%%

## 2. Why Do We Need It?

%%KC_BLOCK%%<section class="convolution-teaching-block convolution-block-response" data-convolution-page="2"><div class="convolution-block-body"><p class="convolution-page-question">Why not just substitute formulas and integrate?</p><ul><li><span class="convolution-key convolution-key-action">Piecewise signals</span> change their overlap rule as \(t\) moves.</li><li><span class="convolution-key convolution-key-input">Graph-only signals</span> may not have a convenient formula.</li><li>The output shape helps us predict <span class="convolution-key convolution-key-output">sampling, filtering, and system memory</span>.</li></ul><figure class="convolution-visual convolution-past-weighting" data-convolution-visual="past-weighting"><figcaption>Figure 2.14 · Past inputs receive different weights at the present time.</figcaption><svg class="convolution-diagram" role="img" aria-labelledby="past-weighting-title" viewBox="0 0 720 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><title id="past-weighting-title">Figure 2.14 relation between past input samples, their remaining system responses, and the output now.</title><line class="convolution-svg-axis" x1="48" y1="170" x2="670" y2="170"/><line class="convolution-svg-cursor" x1="570" y1="42" x2="570" y2="194"/><text class="convolution-svg-fixed-text" x="570" y="28" text-anchor="middle">present t</text><g class="convolution-weight-bars"><line x1="120" y1="170" x2="120" y2="145"/><line x1="220" y1="170" x2="220" y2="128"/><line x1="320" y1="170" x2="320" y2="105"/><line x1="420" y1="170" x2="420" y2="76"/><line x1="520" y1="170" x2="520" y2="50"/></g><path class="convolution-svg-response-line" d="M120 145 C235 137 354 105 520 50"/><text class="convolution-svg-note" x="120" y="216" text-anchor="middle">older input</text><text class="convolution-svg-note" x="520" y="216" text-anchor="middle">recent input</text></svg></figure><p class="convolution-takeaway"><strong>Key idea:</strong> convolution is a moving weighted sum of the past.</p></div></section>%%KC_END%%

## 3. Understanding t and τ

%%KC_BLOCK%%<section class="convolution-teaching-block convolution-block-action" data-convolution-page="3"><div class="convolution-block-body"><p class="convolution-page-question">Which time moves, and which time is being scanned?</p><div class="convolution-role-grid"><div><span class="convolution-role-symbol">\(t\)</span><strong>Output time</strong><p>Freeze it while calculating one value \(c(t)\).</p></div><div><span class="convolution-role-symbol">\(\tau\)</span><strong>Integration variable</strong><p>Let it scan from left to right across both signals.</p></div></div><ul><li>During one scan, \(t\) is a <span class="convolution-key convolution-key-output">fixed parking position</span>.</li><li>Across the whole construction, changing \(t\) creates the next output point.</li></ul><div class="convolution-equation">\(\underbrace{x(\tau)}_{\text{fixed shape}}\;\underbrace{g(t-\tau)}_{\text{shape controlled by }t}\)</div><p class="convolution-takeaway"><strong>Say it aloud:</strong> “tau scans; t chooses the output point.”</p></div></section>%%KC_END%%

## 4. The Five-Step Method

%%KC_BLOCK%%<section class="convolution-teaching-block convolution-block-output" data-convolution-page="4"><div class="convolution-block-body"><p class="convolution-page-question">What sequence works for every graphical convolution?</p><div class="convolution-five-steps" data-convolution-visual="five-steps"><div data-convolution-step="change"><strong>Change</strong><span>Rewrite both signals with \(\tau\).</span></div><div data-convolution-step="flip"><strong>Flip</strong><span>Reflect one signal: \(g(\tau)\to g(-\tau)\).</span></div><div data-convolution-step="slide"><strong>Slide</strong><span>Shift it to make \(g(t-\tau)\).</span></div><div data-convolution-step="multiply"><strong>Multiply</strong><span>Form \(x(\tau)g(t-\tau)\) over the overlap.</span></div><div data-convolution-step="integrate"><strong>Integrate</strong><span>Record the product area as \(c(t)\).</span></div></div><ul><li>Find every value of \(t\) where the overlap rule changes.</li><li>Write one output formula for each interval.</li></ul><p class="convolution-takeaway"><strong>Shortcut:</strong> convolution is commutative, so flip the simpler signal when that saves work.</p></div></section>%%KC_END%%

## 5. Change the Variable

%%KC_BLOCK%%<section class="convolution-teaching-block convolution-block-input" data-convolution-page="5"><div class="convolution-block-body"><p class="convolution-page-question">How do we prepare Figure 2.7 for the integration axis?</p><div class="convolution-equation">\(x(t)=u(t+1),\qquad g(t)=2e^{-(t+2)}u(t+2)\)</div><div class="convolution-equation">\(x(\tau)=u(\tau+1),\qquad g(\tau)=2e^{-(\tau+2)}u(\tau+2)\)</div><ul><li>Only the variable name changes; the shapes do not move yet.</li><li>\(x(\tau)\) begins at \(\tau=-1\).</li><li>\(g(\tau)\) begins at \(\tau=-2\).</li></ul></div></section>%%KC_END%%

%%KC_BLOCK%%<div class="kc-interactive-demo" data-demo-b64=""></div>%%KC_END%%

## 6. Flip

%%KC_BLOCK%%<section class="convolution-teaching-block convolution-block-response" data-convolution-page="6"><div class="convolution-block-body"><p class="convolution-page-question">What exactly changes when we flip \(g(\tau)\)?</p><div class="convolution-equation">\(g(\tau)=2e^{-(\tau+2)}u(\tau+2)\;\longrightarrow\;g(-\tau)=2e^{\tau-2}u(2-\tau)\)</div><ul><li>The boundary at \(-2\) mirrors to \(+2\).</li><li>The right-sided decay becomes a <span class="convolution-key convolution-key-response">left-sided rise</span>.</li><li>The flip happens before any sliding.</li></ul><p class="convolution-takeaway"><strong>Quick check:</strong> if the support did not reverse direction, the flip is incomplete.</p></div></section>%%KC_END%%

%%KC_BLOCK%%<div class="kc-interactive-demo" data-demo-b64=""></div>%%KC_END%%

## 7. Slide

%%KC_BLOCK%%<section class="convolution-teaching-block convolution-block-action" data-convolution-page="7"><div class="convolution-block-body"><p class="convolution-page-question">How does the flipped signal move?</p><div class="convolution-equation">\(g(-\tau)\;\longrightarrow\;g(t-\tau)=2e^{\tau-t-2}u(t+2-\tau)\)</div><div class="convolution-analogy-layout"><div><h3>A farm and a sprinkler truck</h3><ul><li>The crop density along the road is the fixed \(x(\tau)\).</li><li>The truck carries the flipped spray pattern \(g(t-\tau)\).</li><li>Changing \(t\) parks the truck at a new location.</li></ul></div><figure class="convolution-analogy-figure"><img class="lesson-img convolution-analogy-image" src="/lesson-illustrations/2_4-2/convolution-sprinkler-procedure-v2.png" data-api-asset="1" alt="A sprinkler truck sliding across crops with different densities" width="1153" height="2048" loading="lazy" decoding="async"></figure></div><ul><li>The moving boundary is \(\tau=t+2\).</li><li>First contact occurs when \(t+2=-1\), so <span class="convolution-key convolution-key-action">\(t=-3\)</span>.</li></ul></div></section>%%KC_END%%

%%KC_BLOCK%%<div class="kc-interactive-demo" data-demo-b64=""></div>%%KC_END%%

## 8. Multiply and Find the Overlap

%%KC_BLOCK%%<section class="convolution-teaching-block convolution-block-action" data-convolution-page="8"><div class="convolution-block-body"><p class="convolution-page-question">Which part contributes to the output?</p><div class="convolution-equation">\(p_t(\tau)=x(\tau)g(t-\tau)\)</div><ul><li>Outside the overlap, at least one signal is zero, so the product is zero.</li><li>At first contact \(t=-3\), the overlap has zero width.</li><li>For \(t>-3\), the overlap is \(-1\le\tau\le t+2\).</li></ul><div class="convolution-interval-line"><span>fixed boundary \(-1\)</span><i></i><span>moving boundary \(t+2\)</span></div><p class="convolution-takeaway"><strong>Do not measure width alone:</strong> multiply the two heights across the whole interval.</p></div></section>%%KC_END%%

%%KC_BLOCK%%<div class="kc-interactive-demo" data-demo-b64=""></div>%%KC_END%%

## 9. Integrate and Trace the Output

%%KC_BLOCK%%<section class="convolution-teaching-block convolution-block-output" data-convolution-page="9"><div class="convolution-block-body"><p class="convolution-page-question">How does one shaded area become the whole output curve?</p><div class="convolution-equation">\(c(t)=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{t+2}2e^{\tau-t-2}\,d\tau=2\left(1-e^{-(t+3)}\right),\quad t>-3\)</div><div class="convolution-piecewise"><span>\(t\le-3\)</span><strong>\(c(t)=0\)</strong><span>\(t>-3\)</span><strong>\(c(t)=2\left(1-e^{-(t+3)}\right)\)</strong></div><ul><li>Measure the product area at one \(t\).</li><li>Plot that area as the point \((t,c(t))\).</li><li>Move \(t\), repeat, and connect the output points.</li></ul><p class="convolution-takeaway"><strong>Area and output are not two answers:</strong> they are the same number viewed in two places.</p></div></section>%%KC_END%%

%%KC_BLOCK%%<div class="kc-interactive-demo" data-demo-b64=""></div>%%KC_END%%

## 10. Worked Example 1

%%KC_BLOCK%%<section class="convolution-teaching-block convolution-worked-example" data-convolution-page="10"><div class="convolution-block-body"><p class="convolution-page-question">Example 2.10: what happens when two causal exponentials overlap?</p><div class="convolution-equation">\(x(t)=e^{-t}u(t),\qquad g(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)\)</div><ol class="convolution-worked-steps"><li><strong>Support:</strong> both are causal, so the output begins at \(t=0\).</li><li><strong>Overlap:</strong> for \(t>0\), use \(0\le\tau\le t\).</li><li><strong>Integrate:</strong> \(c(t)=\int_0^t e^{-\tau}e^{-2(t-\tau)}d\tau\).</li></ol><div class="convolution-equation convolution-answer">\(c(t)=(e^{-t}-e^{-2t})u(t)\)</div><p class="convolution-takeaway"><strong>Shape check:</strong> it starts at zero, rises, then decays back toward zero.</p></div></section>%%KC_END%%

%%KC_BLOCK%%<div class="kc-interactive-demo" data-demo-b64=""></div>%%KC_END%%

## 11. Worked Example 2

%%KC_BLOCK%%<section class="convolution-teaching-block convolution-worked-example" data-convolution-page="11"><div class="convolution-block-body"><p class="convolution-page-question">Example 2.11: why must the output split at \(t=0\)?</p><div class="convolution-equation">\(x(t)=u(t),\qquad g(t)=\begin{cases}2e^{-t},&t\ge0,\\-2e^{2t},&t<0.\end{cases}\)</div><ul><li>The response changes formula at zero, so the overlap integral must change there too.</li><li>For \(t<0\), only the negative-time branch contributes.</li><li>For \(t\ge0\), the scan includes both response branches.</li></ul><div class="convolution-piecewise"><span>\(t<0\)</span><strong>\(c(t)=-e^{2t}\)</strong><span>\(t\ge0\)</span><strong>\(c(t)=1-2e^{-t}\)</strong></div><p class="convolution-takeaway"><strong>Continuity check:</strong> both formulas give \(-1\) at \(t=0\).</p></div></section>%%KC_END%%

%%KC_BLOCK%%<div class="kc-interactive-demo" data-demo-b64=""></div>%%KC_END%%

## 12. Worked Example 3

%%KC_BLOCK%%<section class="convolution-teaching-block convolution-worked-example" data-convolution-page="12"><div class="convolution-block-body"><p class="convolution-page-question">Example 2.12: how do finite supports predict the whole answer?</p><div class="convolution-equation">\(x(t)=u(t+1)-u(t-1),\qquad g(t)=\frac{t}{3}[u(t)-u(t-3)]\)</div><ul><li>Input support: \([-1,1]\), width 2.</li><li>Response support: \([0,3]\), width 3.</li><li>Output support: <span class="convolution-key convolution-key-output">\([-1,4]\)</span>, width 5.</li><li>The overlap rule changes at \(t=-1,1,2,4\).</li></ul><div class="convolution-piecewise convolution-piecewise-wide"><span>\(-1<t<1\)</span><strong>\(\frac{(t+1)^2}{6}\)</strong><span>\(1\le t<2\)</span><strong>\(\frac{2t}{3}\)</strong><span>\(2\le t<4\)</span><strong>\(\frac{9-(t-1)^2}{6}\)</strong></div><p class="convolution-takeaway"><strong>Support check:</strong> the output must be zero before \(-1\) and after \(4\).</p></div></section>%%KC_END%%

%%KC_BLOCK%%<div class="kc-interactive-demo" data-demo-b64=""></div>%%KC_END%%
